raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old woman visited the hospital for evaluation of facial swelling and fatigue lasting for more than one year. She reported 5 kg of weight gain, hypertension, insomnia, weakness, and easy bruising. She denied any fever, oligouria, chest distress or shortness of breath. She went to the local hospital and the examinations were unremarkable except "hypokalemia." She had been treated with irbesartan at a daily dose of 150 mg for 1 year. The social history and family history was unremarkable.
On examination, the blood pressure was 164/84 mm Hg, the pulse 56 beats per minute, the weight 53.7 kg, the height 146 cm and the body mass index (BMI) 25.19 kg/m2. She had moon face, dorsal fat pad, abdominal obesity and ecchymosis, but no striae. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Initial investigations were summarized in Table 1. A midnight serum cortisol was 16.2 ng/dl and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) was 94.9 pg/ml 24-h urinary free cortisol (UFC) was 813.5 mug/day. Cortisol failed to suppress during a 48-h low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (16.1 ng/dl). These findings were consistent with an ACTH-dependent CS. No suppression was seen with high-dose dexamethasone test. A pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a 1.2 cm adenoma (Figure 1A). Inferior petrosal sinus (IPS) sampling confirmed a pituitary source of ACTH secretion. At the same time, the chest computed tomography revealed multiple lung nodules (Figure 1B). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and serum cryptococcal antigen was positive. Lung biopsy histology confirmed pulmonary Cryptococcus neoformans. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cryptococcal antigen was negative.
Immediate transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy (TSS) was not an option due to cryptococcus infection and possible postoperative cryptococcal meningitis. Intravenous fluconazole was started with 400 mg daily. One week later, the patient was discharged and continued with oral fluconazole 400 mg per day. At 3 months follow-up the pulmonary infection improved and the UFC was 42.2 mug/day. Fluconazole was withdrawn and TSS was performed. Histopathology confirmed ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
Three months after TSS, the patient was in good general health and her serum cortisol and UFC normalized.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old woman presented with a >1-year history of facial swelling, fatigue, a 5-kg weight gain, hypertension, insomnia, weakness, and easy bruising.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding year, the patient experienced progressive facial rounding/swelling, generalized fatigue, a 5-kg weight gain, insomnia, muscle weakness, easy bruising, hypertension, and hypokalemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension and hypokalemia diagnosed 1 year prior; social and family history unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for facial swelling, fatigue, 5-kg weight gain, insomnia, weakness, and easy bruising. Negative for fever, oliguria, chest distress, or dyspnea. Home medication: irbesartan 150 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure 164/84 mmHg, pulse 56 beats/min, weight 53.7 kg, height 146 cm, BMI 25.19 kg/m2. Cushingoid features including moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, central abdominal obesity, and cutaneous ecchymoses without striae.
objective.routine_investigations: Hypokalemia; midnight serum cortisol 16.2 ng/dL, plasma ACTH 94.9 pg/mL, markedly elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) 813.5 ug/day, and non-suppression of cortisol on both 48-hour low-dose (16.1 ng/dL) and high-dose dexamethasone suppression tests. Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Pituitary MRI demonstrated a 1.2 cm pituitary adenoma, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) confirmed a pituitary source of excess ACTH secretion. Chest CT revealed multiple pulmonary nodules; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cryptococcal antigen was positive, and lung biopsy histopathology confirmed pulmonary Cryptococcus neoformans infection, while CSF cryptococcal antigen was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of asymptomatic pulmonary Cryptococcus neoformans infection complicating ACTH-dependent Cushing's disease from a 1.2 cm pituitary corticotroph adenoma, confirmed by positive serum and BALF cryptococcal antigen, lung biopsy histopathology, pituitary MRI/IPSS, and subsequent surgical adenoma histopathology (with CNS cryptococcosis ruled out by negative CSF CrAg). Transsphenoidal surgery was deferred for 3 months while the patient was treated with fluconazole 400 mg daily (IV for 1 week, then oral), resulting in radiographic pulmonary improvement and reduction of 24-hour UFC from 813.5 to 42.2 ug/day; she then underwent curative transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy with complete normalization of serum and urinary cortisol at 3-month postoperative follow-up.
